strengths: Introduces a well-motivated collaborative trajectory formulation that decomposes robotic manipulation into pre-interaction, interaction, and post-interaction phases, directly targeting the feature entanglement problem in overlapping regions.
Combines mask-based object embeddings with appearance and shape cues, and incorporates causal latent propagation to improve subject identity consistency across generated frames.

Provides extensive experiments on Bridge V2 with multiple trajectory-controlled baselines, user study, VBench metrics, and diverse ablation studies, showing consistent improvements over prior methods.
Demonstrates practical user interaction advantages, including robustness to coarse brush masks and trajectory perturbations, which is valuable for real-world annotation workflows.
Qualitative results on in-the-wild images and diverse manipulation skills illustrate generalization beyond the training distribution.
weaknesses: The core novelty is incremental: phase-wise decomposition and dominant-object conditioning are intuitive heuristics, and the motion injection design largely follows existing trajectory-conditioned video diffusion approaches.

The evaluation is limited to video generation metrics and does not validate the central motivation of generating robotic decision-making data, e.g., no downstream policy learning or action prediction experiments.

The Trajectory Error metric is not fully specified: it is unclear how generated robot/object trajectories are extracted, which weakens reproducibility and interpretability of the reported trajectory accuracy.

The claimed shape-aware object representation is limited to a circular volume whose radius is proportional to mask area, rather than encoding actual object shape, which may overstate the method's shape awareness.

Quantitative gains over the strongest baselines are modest on FVD, PSNR, SSIM, and VBench, and no significance tests or variance estimates are provided; the user study protocol and participant details are also missing.
The manuscript contains an incomplete loss equation (Equation 7 ends with 'where' without definitions) and vague descriptions of the causal embedding and motion injection details.
Evaluation is primarily on a single quantitative dataset (Bridge V2); in-the-wild validation is qualitative, and baseline retraining configurations are only partially described in the main text.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: controllable video generation for robotic manipulation and data augmentation.

The collaborative trajectory idea (decomposing interaction into pre-interaction, interaction, and post-interaction phases) is intuitive and may reduce feature entanglement compared with treating robot and object trajectories independently.
The mask-based object embedding is simple and supports user-friendly annotation, with demonstrated robustness to coarse masks and trajectory perturbation.
The paper reports experiments on the Bridge V2 dataset with several trajectory-control baselines, VBench metrics, user study, and ablations, which provides some evidence for the proposed design.
Qualitative in-the-wild examples and the Gradio annotation interface illustrate potential practical usability.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the method largely combines existing components—trajectory conditioning, mask-based object embeddings, phase decomposition, and a motion injector similar to prior work such as Tora/ControlNet—without a fundamental technical advance.

The central claim that the method enables video generation as an interactive simulator for producing robotic decision-making data is not supported by downstream policy learning or real-robot experiments; evaluation is limited to video quality and trajectory-error metrics.
Evaluation is narrow: only Bridge V2 is used quantitatively (214 test samples), in-the-wild results are qualitative only, and there is no multi-dataset or cross-embodiment quantitative validation.

Baseline comparisons are potentially unfair or incomplete: all baselines are retrained on CogVideoX-5B, which may not reflect their optimal configurations, and recent trajectory-control methods such as 3DTrajMaster, LeviTor, and ObjCtrl-2.5D are not compared despite being discussed.
Some claims overreach the evidence: VBench improvements are small, user-study preference is a plurality rather than a majority, and no statistical significance or confidence intervals are reported.

Method presentation has clarity and reproducibility issues: notation in Eqs. (3)–(4) is inconsistent, Eq. (7) does not clearly include the object latent variables, and it is unclear how the factorized sub-distributions in Eq. (5) are combined during sampling.
The “shape-aware” representation is weak: shape is encoded only as a circular radius derived from mask area, not as actual object shape, so the claimed shape awareness is overstated.

Physical plausibility is not adequately evaluated: there is no contact/force consistency check, and conditioning on object motion during interaction to guide the robot may not ensure physically valid robot-object interaction.

Ablations are limited: mask sparsity and trajectory perturbation are reported only as relative PSNR without trajectory error or other metrics, and there is no ablation on phase decomposition granularity, radius choice, or embedding design.

Generalization is limited by the requirement of a pre-defined or automatically extracted robot-arm mask and by the purely 2D formulation; the paper acknowledges these limitations but does not resolve them.

strengths: Introduces a novel collaborative trajectory formulation that decomposes robotic manipulation into pre-interaction, interaction, and post-interaction phases, with dominant-subject-aware feature control. This directly addresses feature entanglement in overlapping regions during robot-object interaction.
Combines collaborative trajectories with appearance- and shape-aware mask-based object embeddings, preserving manipulated object identity and enabling more intuitive user annotation.
Reports state-of-the-art results on the Bridge V2 benchmark across multiple metrics, including FVD, PSNR, SSIM, trajectory error, VBench scores, and a user preference study.

Provides thorough ablations validating the contributions of causal embedding, mask-based representation, collaborative trajectory design, and motion injection, as well as robustness to mask sparsity and trajectory perturbation.
Demonstrates qualitative generalization to in-the-wild images and diverse manipulation skills, showing practical promise for generating robotic training data.
weaknesses: The quantitative gains over strong baselines such as Tora are modest on some video quality metrics (e.g., FVD, PSNR, SSIM), though the user study and trajectory error improvements are more compelling.
In-the-wild evaluation is primarily qualitative; there is no quantitative benchmark for out-of-domain scenarios or diverse robot embodiments, so the generalization claim is not fully measured.
The method still relies on user-provided object masks and interaction phase boundaries, and the robot arm mask is assumed to be available or predefined, which may limit fully automatic deployment.
Reproducibility could be strengthened by releasing code or more detailed data curation scripts; currently the paper describes training details but not code availability.

Some equations and notation are not fully clear (e.g., indexing in Eq. 3, notation in Eq. 7), and the method section could better formalize how latent trajectory coordinates are mapped to the circular volume representation.

strengths: Introduces a collaborative trajectory formulation that decomposes manipulation into pre-interaction, interaction, and post-interaction phases, providing a clear and intuitive way to reduce feature entanglement between robot and object trajectories.

Proposes mask-based object embeddings that encode both appearance and shape via a circular volumetric representation, enabling robust user interaction with coarse brush masks and improving subject consistency.
Conducts extensive experiments across Bridge, RLBench, SIMPLER, and VBench, with retrained baselines and downstream robotic action planning, providing broad empirical support.
Contributes a 21k video-trajectory dataset from Bridge with an automatic human-in-the-loop annotation pipeline, which may benefit future robotic video generation research.

Includes useful ablation studies on causal embedding, mask vs. point representation, trajectory injection design, mask sparsity, trajectory perturbation, and imperfect prompts, and acknowledges limitations such as 2D-only control and morphology generalization.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the method largely combines existing ideas such as trajectory-conditioned video diffusion, mask-based object embeddings, and phase decomposition, rather than introducing a fundamentally new paradigm.

Quantitative gains over the strongest baseline, Tora, are relatively modest on the main video quality and trajectory metrics (e.g., FVD 147.31 vs. 152.28, object TrajError 24.16 vs. 26.43), and the ablation w/ Separate Trajectories is close to the full model, weakening the claim that collaborative trajectory control is dramatically better.

The collaborative formulation still conditions on one subject at a time per phase and models robot-object coupling mainly implicitly through the manipulated object's trajectory during interaction; it does not explicitly model simultaneous interaction dynamics, so feature entanglement may not be fully resolved.

Downstream action planning results are mixed: RoboMaster is not best on several tasks (e.g., put knife and open microwave under RLBench), and the average RLBench improvement over Tora is marginal, which does not fully support the claim of consistent superiority.
The user study is reported only as a preference percentage without protocol details, participant count, or evaluation criteria, making it difficult to assess reliability and potential bias.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or dataset release is mentioned, inverse dynamics model details are sparse, and the automatic annotation pipeline has low success rates for multi-object scenes, requiring substantial manual correction and limiting scalability.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: controllable video generation for robotic manipulation, where scalable data is a key bottleneck.
The collaborative trajectory decomposition into pre-interaction, interaction, and post-interaction phases is intuitive and motivated by observed failure modes of prior trajectory-controlled methods.
Mask-based object embeddings with appearance sampling and radius-based spatial expansion improve identity preservation over point-based baselines, as shown qualitatively and in ablations.
Experiments span Bridge, RLBench, and SIMPLER, with multiple trajectory-controlled baselines, VBench metrics, user study, and robustness ablations, giving a reasonably broad evaluation picture.
The paper contributes a curated 21k video-trajectory dataset from Bridge, which could be useful for future work if released and validated.
The presentation is generally clear, with a detailed appendix covering dataset construction and additional qualitative results.
weaknesses: The central technical novelty is incremental and somewhat misleading. The method does not truly model a joint collaborative trajectory; it switches between dominant and submissive trajectories across phases and ignores the robot-arm trajectory during the interaction phase, so the claimed 'unified' joint motion is only partially realized.

The 'shape-aware' object representation is weakly supported. The circular volume is constructed using only the mask area as radius, which discards actual object shape; for elongated or irregular objects this is a crude proxy. No ablation isolates shape encoding from appearance or area.

Quantitative gains over the strongest baseline, Tora, are marginal: FVD 147.31 vs. 152.28, PSNR 21.55 vs. 21.24, SSIM 0.803 vs. 0.788. This is a narrow margin for a top-tier venue and may not justify the claims of clear superiority.

The trajectory error metric is under-specified: the paper does not explain how generated trajectories are extracted, whether tracking is manual/automatic, or how errors are computed for both arm and object. This limits reproducibility and interpretation.

The action-planning comparison does not support the claim of consistent improvement. RoboMaster loses to Tora on important tasks such as 'put knife' (0.76 vs. 0.82) and 'open microwave' (0.54 vs. 0.61), and the text claims '8 out of 10' tasks despite reporting 9 tasks and only 7/9 wins. Success rates are simulated and generally modest.

Dataset curation quality is questionable: Grounded-SAM annotation success is low (0.67 single-object, 0.14 multi-object), requiring manual re-annotation for thousands of videos. The resulting labels may be noisy, and the paper does not report annotation quality or inter-annotator agreement.

Reproducibility is limited: no code/dataset release is indicated, and several key details are missing, including the motion threshold tau for interaction decoupling, inverse dynamics model training details, user-study protocol, and trajectory extraction procedure.

Robustness claims rely on PSNR reported as a relative percentage under mask sparsity, trajectory perturbation, and imperfect prompts; the protocol and baselines for these tables are unclear, making the strong robustness conclusions hard to verify.

The user study is only reported as a preference percentage without details on participant count, interface, instructions, or statistical significance, so it provides weak evidence for the large claimed preference gap.

strengths: Introduces a novel collaborative trajectory formulation that decomposes robotic manipulation into pre-interaction, interaction, and post-interaction phases, using the dominant object (robot arm) for pre/post phases and the manipulated object during interaction. This directly addresses feature entanglement in overlapping regions that plagues prior separate-trajectory methods.

The mask-based appearance- and shape-aware object embedding (circular volumetric representation) is simple yet effective, improving object identity consistency and enabling robust user annotation with coarse masks.

Extensive and well-structured empirical validation: state-of-the-art results on Bridge for video quality and trajectory accuracy, additional VBench comparisons, RLBench and SIMPLER action-planning evaluations, user study, and thorough ablations (causal embedding, point vs. mask representation, separate vs. collaborative trajectory, cross-attention injection, mask sparsity, trajectory perturbation, imperfect prompts).
Demonstrates practical user interactivity, requiring only an object mask and decomposed sub-trajectories rather than full arm-object trajectories, and shows robustness to imprecise user inputs.
Provides good reproducibility details: architecture table, implementation hyperparameters, dataset curation pipeline, and a Gradio demo description.
Meaningful contribution to video generation as a world simulator for robotic manipulation, with potential to alleviate data scarcity and improve downstream policy learning.
weaknesses: Quantitative gains over the strongest baseline (Tora) are modest (FVD 152.28 -> 147.31, PSNR 21.24 -> 21.55, SSIM 0.788 -> 0.803), and action-planning success rates are mixed: RoboMaster underperforms Tora on two RLBench tasks (put knife and open microwave), so claims of consistent improvement are somewhat overstated.
The user study lacks important details (number of participants, protocol, confidence intervals, task selection), making the 45.16% vs. 17.74% preference margin hard to assess rigorously.

Some robustness results appear surprisingly high (e.g., 90% mask sparsity retains 99.81% PSNR; 20% trajectory deviation retains 97.15% PSNR), which may indicate that the evaluation metrics are insensitive or that the model relies heavily on the initial frame rather than the object embedding. More analysis would strengthen these claims.

Novelty is incremental: the core components (trajectory-conditioned video generation, mask/entity-based object representation, motion injection) build directly on prior work such as Tora and DragAnything. The main advance is the phase-decomposition strategy and its combination with mask embeddings, which is more engineering-oriented than fundamentally new.

The term 'collaborative trajectory' is somewhat overclaimed: the method effectively uses phase-wise object-specific trajectories rather than a truly unified joint trajectory, and the interaction phase relies only on the manipulated object's trajectory to implicitly guide the robot arm.
No code or dataset release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility despite detailed implementation descriptions.

The action-planning evaluation is indirect, depending on a separately trained inverse dynamics model and a post-trained action-conditioned video model. Direct comparison to policies trained on real demonstrations would provide stronger evidence.
